transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Arbor Lead Eng), Priya Patel (Arbor Platform), Daniel Wu (CTO)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): quick pairing to get SDKs installed in python + ts, wire auth, and demo console/optimize. Focus on CI secrets and VPC/KMS questions.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE on this account. Priya D is our SE — she'll lead the hands-on. can you all hear ok?
[00:12] Liam (Arbor): yeah, loud and clear. thanks. quick note we've got Priya P from platform and Daniel on for architecture questions.
[00:20] Priya D (Redwood SE): awesome. goal for today is to pair on installing the SDKs (python + typescript), walk through auth patterns (api keys vs sso), wire env vars and CI secrets (Vault / GHA), and then show Redwood Console routes and a couple Optimize recommendations for batching.
[00:34] Daniel (CTO): sounds good. our immediate blocker is secrets rotation and KMS integration — we are locked down around key management and need to verify no plaintext keys in repo.
[00:45] Priya D: totally, we'll show patterns that avoid checkins, e.g. short-lived tokens from your KMS or HashiCorp Vault and token rotation. Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for hosted we can integrate CMK via provider.
[00:58] Liam: good. also curious about our CI (github actions) flow — is there a recommended way to store the API key? we use GHA with repo-level secrets and some workflows in a shared org runner.
[01:10] Priya D: common approach: store a short-lived API token in Vault, then GHA pulls it at job-start. alternatively use a GitHub Actions OIDC flow to exchange for a token in your auth infra, then call Redwood with that ephemeral token. we can show a small example.
[01:28] Jordan: ok let's start with the python SDK install. Priya, can you share your screen and open the quickstart?
[01:37] Priya D: sure — switching screens. (screen share) npm i @redwood/inference-client or pip install redwood-inference — note package names are sometimes confused in transcripts, it's redwood-inference on pip.
[01:52] Priya P (Arbor): small nit — do we have a pinned version recommended for production?
[01:58] Priya D: yes, we recommend pinning the minor version, e.g. 2.4.x, and we publish release notes in the changelog. for critical infra we suggest using the semver lock and a lockfile.
[02:10] Liam: when using the SDK, where does the API key live in the runtime?
[02:17] Priya D: typical pattern: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env vars on the host or container runtime. for serverless you inject via secrets manager at runtime. avoid baking into image. also mention token rotation via Redwood token endpoint if you want to mint ephemeral tokens.
[02:33] Daniel: can we use SSO for service accounts? we want RBAC tied to Okta groups.
[02:41] Jordan: yes — Redwood supports SSO (SAML/OIDC) for user access and has service principals for programmatic access that can be linked to SSO providers and group-based RBAC, though the exact flows differ between hosted and Private. we'll send the SSO mapping doc.
[02:56] Priya D: demo time: quick python snippet — (typing) from redwood_inference import Client
client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate('Summarize this...')
print(resp.text)

Note: transcript may mangle underscores or module names.
[03:32] Liam: ok that looks straightforward. show the TS flow?
[03:38] Priya D: switching — typescript quickstart: import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'
const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
await client.generate({ prompt: '...' })

(Background chatter: someone says "node version 18 is what we use")
[03:58] Liam: question about streaming — we do real-time chat, need lower latency. how do we stream tokens?
[04:05] Priya D: SDKs support SSE / websockets and streaming endpoints. for node the client exposes an on('token') handler. for python we expose an iterator that yields tokens. streaming is available on hosted and Dedicated; on Private you may need to enable the streaming gateway depending on network setup.
[04:29] Daniel: any difference to enable streaming in terms of auth or CORS?
[04:33] Priya D: no special auth, same token. CORS is relevant for browser-based flows — we generally recommend proxying from a backend or using short-lived browser tokens via your auth provider.
[04:50] Jordan: let's pivot to Console — I'll share a quick tour of routes, quotas, and Optimize suggestions.
[04:58] (screen share) Jordan: here's the Console route config — you can create a route per product surface, pin a model version, and set batching windows and KV cache TTLs. you can also attach a fallback model for graceful degradation.
[05:22] Priya P: is there a UI control for max tokens or per-request cost limits?
[05:27] Jordan: yes — per-route max tokens and per-request cost caps. we also show estimated per-token cost based on model and quantization.
[05:36] Liam: Optimize — we want recommended batching and quantization settings for our user traffic that has short prompts but high QPS. what does that look like?
[05:45] Priya D: Optimize runs workload sampling — it will recommend batch sizes, KV cache usage, and a quantization profile (e.g. int8 vs int4) based on latency targets. for short prompts, small batch sizes with a lower batching window are better; we can tune autoscaling policy on Dedicated to handle QPS spikes.
[06:05] Daniel: if we do Dedicated trial, what's the onboarding like and network setup? we need to keep traffic inside our VPC.
[06:13] Jordan: Dedicated gives reserved GPUs and can be VPC-peered or delivered via Private. for strict network isolation, Private deployment inside your VPC or on-prem package is available; that supports CMK and HSM integrations. We'll coordinate infra details with your platform team.
[06:34] Liam: perfect. can we run a quick test — provision a sandbox and run a basic batch to see latency?
[06:41] Jordan: yeah, we'll provision a sandbox tenant. Priya D, I think you can hand them a temporary key and a small test script.
[06:47] Priya D: doing that now — I'll paste the key example into the chat but not the real key in the transcript. Example script: run python tests/batch_ping.py --keys env. For TS, run node tests/batch_ping.js. We'll include sample load script to simulate 50 rps.
[07:05] Priya P: our CI question — how to instrument tests without exposing keys to forks? We have public forks occasionally.
[07:13] Priya D: avoid repo secrets used by forks using protected env or require PRs to run tests on internal runner. better: ephemeral keys from Vault or use GHA OIDC to exchange and restrict by repo/branch. we'll attach a GHA example in the notes.
[07:30] Liam: security folks will want audit logs and usage telemetry per token. do you provide token-level traces?
[07:36] Jordan: yes, Console has token-level traces, per-route request logs, and an audit log for admin actions. logs can be exported to your SIEM. We also have event hooks for trace sampling.
[07:50] Daniel: about data retention and PII — can we configure retention windows and redaction?
[07:56] Priya D: retention policies are configurable in Dedicated/Private and for hosted we have configurable retention tiers. PII redaction and redact-at-ingest patterns can be used; we'll share the security pack that explains retention and redaction.
[08:10] Jordan: quick aside — competitor question: some teams try to roll their own inference; we talked about cost and ops overhead earlier in the RFP. Redwood's Optimize and autoscaling try to reduce unit costs compared to a naive self-hosted pipeline.
[08:27] Liam: that ties into our numbers. ok let's run through a short perf checklist you mentioned.
[08:33] Priya D: perf checklist: sample distribution (seq lengths), target p99 latency, batching window, quantization profile, KV cache hit rate targets, and autoscale headroom. I'll attach a template.
[08:45] (background: brief pause while files are located)
[08:53] Priya D: sending links in chat: SDK quickstart, GHA OIDC example, Vault pattern, and the perf checklist.
[09:00] Liam: saw the links, thanks. one more question — are there rate limits per tenant, and how do we request raises for production?
[09:07] Jordan: hosted tenants have soft quotas and rate limits; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and SLA-backed targets. for production we'll work with your account team to size and set quotas.
[09:18] Priya P: curious about metrics — can we emit request traces to our Datadog?
[09:23] Priya D: yes, you can forward logs or use our tracing hooks; we support OTLP/Jaeger/Datadog export.
[09:33] Daniel: network topology for Private — curious if we need direct peering or an appliance.
[09:38] Jordan: options include VPC peering, PrivateLink, or an on-prem appliance for air-gapped installs. we'll map those to your network restrictions in the follow-up.
[09:52] Liam: ok, back to hands-on — Priya can you show an example .env and github actions snippet?
[09:57] Priya D: yep. .env.example: REDWOOD_API_KEY=<<set in runtime>>
GHA snippet:
- name: Get token
  uses: hashicorp/vault-action@v2
  with:
    url: ${{ secrets.VAULT_ADDR }}
    method: token
- name: Run tests
  env:
    REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ steps.vault.outputs.token }}
  run: pytest tests/ --maxfail=1
Note: if you use OIDC remove static secrets and exchange via your idp.
[10:25] Priya P: couple of scribbles from security: will need to see KMS key policy example and how rotation hooks work.
[10:33] Priya D: on rotation — Redwood can accept rotated keys via CMK integration or you can rotate your short-lived tokens in Vault. We'll include rotation playbook.
[10:45] Jordan: doing a quick recap before we end — action items and next steps. we'll provision sandbox, send keys and README, share security pack and SSO mapping, attach GHA + Vault examples, and schedule benchmark next week.
[10:58] Liam: that's perfect. Daniel: any last questions?
[11:03] Daniel: please include the Dedicated sizing doc.
[11:07] Jordan: will do. thanks everyone — wrap up in 2.
[11:10] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: medium — occasional word swaps and module name punctuation issues.
